001_1947-07-26_Saybrook, Illinois (front.report_summary:
**Document:** FBI Office Memorandum, Standard Form No. 64, from the SAC, Springfield, to the Director, FBI, dated August 20, 1947. The memo references Bureau Bulletin No. 42 (Series 1947), dated July 30, 1947, and carries internal file markings for FBI case 62-0-1445 / SI File 62-0-1445. The second page is the enclosure cover sheet: “Photographs of ‘Flying Disc’ found at Saybrook, Ill. 7-26-47,” indicating six photos enclosed.

**Witness:** Mrs. June Anderson of Saybrook, Illinois, reported the discovery to the Springfield FBI office. The memo gives no indication that she was a trained observer; instead, an agent’s follow-up inquiry notes that her “stability” was questionable, suggesting the reporting circumstances were somewhat unreliable or at least informal.

**Sighting:** The reported event occurred at about 6:00 A.M. on July 26, 1947, when Mrs. Anderson found a “flying disc” in her front yard. The enclosure and memo identify the location only as Saybrook, Illinois.

**Object:** The object was not an aerial craft. Investigation found it to be an old wooden platter with a silver plate, a spark plug, a timer, and pieces of old brass tubing attached. The agent concluded it was apparently assembled from parts gathered by juveniles in the area. The memo explicitly states, “No doubt this was someone’s idea of a prank.”

**Investigation:** Springfield retained the disc pending Bureau guidance, noting that Washington might want to examine it for any novel value. Six photographs were taken and enclosed. The report is therefore best understood as a prank-object recovery case rather than a genuine UFO encounter, despite the contemporary “flying disc” terminology.

**Document:** Single-page correspondence on State of Vermont Department of Education letterhead (Orange-Windsor District, South Royalton), addressed to the Federal Bureau of Investigation in Washington, D.C. **Sighting:** Parker states that at 3:40 P.M. on September 17, 1947, while halfway up Rix Ledges north of Lebanon, New Hampshire, he was watching honey bees near his bee box when he noticed a floating object. He describes the first object as roughly the size of a tennis ball and as white as cotton batting. It approached rapidly and noiselessly from the east.

**Object:** A second object, "in size and shape like a saucer," followed closely behind the first, maintaining a constant angle of inclination and a constant distance. Parker estimated the pair were about five degrees from his eye and remained visible for more than a minute before he lost them in the glare of the sun. In closing, he wrote that if he had seen them at night through his telescope, he would have thought Venus and Saturn had suddenly come together and were traveling at great speed much nearer the earth.

**Assessment:** This page contains the full sighting narrative and no later-page continuation. No FBI conclusion or technical identification appears here; the report preserves the witness's observations and his astronomical analogy only.

**Document:** FBI Office Memorandum, U.S. Government, from SAC Portland to the Director, dated 9-13-47, subject "Flying Discs / Security Matter - X." The page cites an earlier teletype of 9-4-47 and carries internal file markings including 62-1531 and the main case file 62-HQ-83894. No signer is shown on the page; it is an internal investigative report rather than a public statement.

**Witness:** Mrs. Raymond Dupuis of Oswego, Oregon was interviewed by the Portland office. She had been outside on her lawn with her 7-year-old son and a 10-year-old neighbor child when the incident occurred. The memo presents her as a direct eyewitness, with the children as contemporaneous observers, but no additional corroborating witnesses are named on this page.

**Sighting:** On 9-3-47, around noon, the group noticed approximately two dozen round silver objects high in the sky above Oswego. Mrs. Dupuis said they looked platter-shaped rather than spherical, seemed larger than a nearby cub-type airplane, and appeared to be far away and made of a white metallic material. The objects were grouped in an arc about level with and to the left of the sun. She reported that they held position for roughly 3 to 4 minutes, though some of the larger ones rotated rapidly "in the manner of a wheel." One object separated from the group, descended slowly, and disappeared behind trees on the horizon.

**Investigation:** The memo records that the witness initially thought the objects might be skywriting, but she later abandoned that explanation. She kept watching until glare from the bright sky affected her eyes and then went indoors, unable to say what became of the remaining objects. The page contains no formal analysis or identification, only the witness account transmitted up the FBI chain of command as a "security matter" UFO report.

The page carries later FBI routing/index stamps and file references including **62-1531** and a copy to **San Francisco (62-2938)**, indicating this is a field-office summary rather than a direct witness statement.

001_1947-07-31_Tacoma, Washington (Winth.report_summary:
**Document:** This is page three of a typed FBI memorandum in case 62-HQ-83894, Section 2, with handwritten correction marks and a page stamp reading “PAGE THREE.” The visible page continues a longer investigative report; no separate signature block or document date appears on this page.

**Witness/Subjects:** The page centers on Kenneth Arnold (pilot and principal subject of the wider disk-fragment story), along with Dahl, Chrisman, Emil Smith, Ray Palmer, and Ernie Vogel of United Press. It does not record a direct UFO observation on this page; instead, it summarizes telephone contacts and follow-up statements tied to the Arnold-related disc-fragment controversy.

**Incident:** According to the memorandum, on July 31 and August 1 Arnold called Ray Palmer at Evanston, Illinois, and Boise, Idaho, and on August 1 he also called Palmer in Chicago. The page further states that Emil Smith called Roddy in Chicago. It then reports that five anonymous telephone calls were received by a Tacoma Times reporter and a United Press wire man in Tacoma, giving information about a Winthrop Hotel meeting concerning disk fragments and asserting that a B-25 had been shot down or sabotaged, killing Captain Davidson and Lieutenant Brown. The calls implied the plane may have been targeted because intelligence officers were carrying disk fragments.

**Investigation:** Dahl and Chrisman denied making the calls, saying they could only have come from themselves, Smith, or Arnold. The memo says no record could be found of the calls originating from Arnold’s Winthrop Hotel room, and it characterizes Dahl and Chrisman as evasive about what information they provided by phone or letter to Ray Palmer. Overall, the page reads as an FBI attempt to trace rumor sources and phone contacts surrounding the Arnold disk story, rather than as confirmation of any aerial object or confirmed sabotage.

Nelson, Special Agent, CIC 4AF, from an interview with Captain William H. Ryherd at the 415th AAF BU, Building 95, Hamilton Field, California. The page is marked confidential and later declassified under NND 90986.

**Witness:** Primary witness was Capt. William H. Ryherd (ASN O-66356), assistant operations officer in the 415th AAF BU and instructor pilot in the 415th Training Unit. He was accompanied by student 1st Lt. Ward L. Stewart during the sighting.

**Sighting:** On 29 July 1947 at about 1450, after landing an AT-6 near the hangar at Hamilton Field, Ryherd looked west over the hangar and saw a P-80 flying southward toward Oakland. Above the P-80, at roughly 8,000 to 10,000 feet, he observed two flying objects moving in the same direction. He estimated them at about 15 to 25 feet in diameter and described them as solid, white, somewhat shiny, and circular, “like a ball on the bottom, but not completely round.” He specifically said they were not airplanes.

**Object:** The first object moved straight and level; the second followed close behind at the same altitude, alternating left-to-right and right-to-left in a way that resembled an aircraft in formation. Ryherd said their speed made the P-80 appear motionless by comparison. The sky was clear, and the objects disappeared in flight, supposedly over Oakland, heading toward the ocean.

**Investigation:** No sound was heard, though the P-80’s noise may have masked it. Ryherd reported no vapor, smoke, or visible trail. He also said he had told no one before because he feared people would think he was crazy. The agent’s note states Ryherd showed extreme sincerity and answered questions with caution and assurance.

The file copy includes recording/indexing marks, enclosure notation for photos, and later file stamps showing the copies were destroyed in 1964.

Newcomb told FBI Agent SA Richard D. Auerbach that, at about 10:30 p.m., an unknown woman telephoned in an excited state and said the disc had dropped into her garden at 11858 Magnolia Boulevard. Brown of 6552 Teesdale Avenue said he heard neighborhood talk at a service station and believed local students may have been involved in making the object.

**Investigation/Conclusion:** SA Auerbach arranged photos and forwarded them for Bureau inspection. The object was later turned over to Major Courtney W. Hempstead, A.C., G-2, Fort MacArthur, San Pedro, who reported it was definitely a hoax and could not have flown under its own power. The memo’s overall conclusion is that the North Hollywood “flying disc” was fabricated rather than a genuine aerial craft.

**Witness:** 写信人在信末签署了一个部分可辨的姓名，读作“L. C. Hersch”（或非常相近），并给出了 Jersey City, N.J. 的回邮地址（349 Central Ave.）。写信人自述为目击者，并以自己的话报告了这一事件。

**Sighting:** 他称自己于 1947 年 7 月 4 日在 Asbury Park 看到了一枚所谓的“Flying Discs”。他认为它可能是从那里那个舞厅起飞的，但随后它离开了该区域，沿着海岸线向北，在远处消失。

**Object:** 起初，这个物体被认为可能是一个气球，但目击者称它沿着明确的方向移动，速度看起来基本恒定，并且逐渐上升。他将其轨迹比作子弹的飞行轨迹，但“更为明显”。未给出其大小、颜色、声音或持续时间。

**Investigation:** 这一页是向 FBI 提供的非请求性线索，而非正式外勤报告。内容带有主观性，且未经证实，但保留了 1947 年 7 月初在 Asbury Park 木板步道/舞厅区域附近对飞碟目击的一份同期描述。页面本身未显示任何分析结论。

001_1947-07-01_Trail Creek, near Sun Val.report_summary:
**Document:** This page is a Standard Form 64 Office Memorandum from the FBI field office at Butte to the Director, FBI, dated July 3, 1947, on the subject line **FLYING DISCS**. It is part of FBI file 62-HQ-83894, Section 1, and bears internal routing/stamp marks including EX-46 and later file handling stamps. The memorandum records a telephone inquiry rather than a direct field interview.

**Witness/Source:** The named source is **Mr. Dave Johnson** of the *Idaho Daily Statesman* (Boise, Idaho), who telephonically contacted the Butte office. Johnson was acting as a newspaper reporter and information conduit, not as an eyewitness to the event itself. He stated that many citizens had reported seeing the discs and that he believed the reports were not imaginary.

**Sighting:** Johnson said the discs were seen on **July 1, 1947**, in the **vicinity of Trail Creek near Sun Valley, Idaho**, by “reputable citizens.” No individual eyewitness names, number of objects, duration, direction of travel, altitude, color, sound, or speed are given on this page.

**Investigation:** The memo says the FBI office told Johnson it was **not making an investigation** and asked whether he had contacted Army and Navy officials; Johnson replied that he was inquiring of those agencies. The page therefore documents a public rumor/report being relayed through a journalist, not a verified FBI investigation. The evidentiary value is limited because the actual witnesses are unnamed and the description is secondhand.

**Witness/Source:** 所署名的来源是 *Idaho Daily Statesman*（Boise, Idaho）的 **Mr. Dave Johnson**，他通过电话联系了 Butte 办公室。Johnson 当时的身份是报社记者和信息转述者，而不是事件本身的目击者。他表示，许多市民都报告看到了这些飞碟，并且他认为这些报告并非凭空想象。

**Sighting:** Johnson 称，这些飞碟于 **1947年7月1日**，在 **Trail Creek near Sun Valley, Idaho** 附近被“信誉良好的公民”看到。该页未给出任何具体目击者姓名、物体数量、持续时间、飞行方向、飞行高度、颜色、声音或速度。

001_1947-07-07_Shreveport, Louisiana (Te.report_summary:
**Document:** One-page FBI New Orleans teletype, marked “VERY URGENT,” dated 7-7-47 at 8:02 PM, from the FBI Communications Section to the Director, FBI. The subject line reads “FLYING DISCS, MISCELLANEOUS.” The page contains no continuation marker, so this single page is the full report used here.

**Witness:** F. C. Hairston of 1554 Texas Avenue, Shreveport, Louisiana. He is identified only as a civilian observer, not as a trained aviation or scientific witness. The report says he notified military personnel at Barksdale Field immediately after recovering the object.

**Sighting:** Hairston reported seeing a circular disc at about 6:05 PM on 7 July 1947, coming from the northwest. He said it landed in the 1500 block of Texas Avenue, and that he picked it up at 1554 Texas Avenue. He described the object as whirling in flight, with fire “spouting from sides.” The fire stopped on landing, and smoke appeared a few seconds later. He stated the disc was not hot when recovered.

**Object:** The FBI teletype describes a thin aluminum disc about 16 inches in diameter, with small coils about 2 inches in diameter and 4 inches long at the ends of the diameter. Two copper wires connected the coils to terminals and to a center object about 1 inch in diameter and 2 inches long, likened to a fluorescent-light starter. The center bore the words “MADE IN USA,” and the object reportedly made a sound like a policeman’s whistle. The underside was described as the smooth side facing earth in flight.

**Investigation:** Barksdale Field personnel reportedly took custody of the disc before an FBI Special Agent arrived, and they were making photographs. The message says Barksdale would turn the item over to the FBI if desired, subject to superior instructions, and that the names of all persons who handled it before the agent’s arrival were secured. The report strongly suggests a recovered man-made device or component rather than an unidentified aerial craft, but the document does not record a final technical identification.
001_1947-07-07_Shreveport, Louisiana (Te.report_summary_zh:

**Witness:** F. C. Hairston，住址为路易斯安那州什里夫波特(Shreveport, Louisiana) Texas Avenue 1554号。他仅被认定为一名普通目击者，并非受过训练的航空或科学证人。报告称，他在取回该物体后立即通知了Barksdale Field的军方人员。

**Sighting:** Hairston报告称，他于1947年7月7日约下午6:05看到一个圆盘自西北方向飞来。他说该物体降落在Texas Avenue 1500号街区，并且他是在Texas Avenue 1554号将其拾起的。他描述该物体在飞行中旋转，并有火焰“从两侧喷出”。物体着陆后火焰停止，几秒钟后出现了烟雾。他表示，取回时该圆盘并不烫手。

**Object:** FBI电传件将其描述为一个薄铝制圆盘，直径约16英寸，在直径两端各有一个直径约2英寸、长4英寸的小线圈。两根铜线将线圈连接到端子以及一个位于中心、直径约1英寸、长2英寸的物件上，该中心部件被比作荧光灯启动器。中心部位印有“MADE IN USA”字样，据称该物体发出的声音类似警察口哨。其底面被描述为飞行时朝向地球的一面，表面光滑。

**Investigation:** 据称，在FBI Special Agent到达之前，Barksdale Field的人员已接管该圆盘，并正在拍照。电报称，如有需要，Barksdale将按上级指示把该物品移交给FBI，并且在该探员到达前经手此物的所有人员姓名都已记录在案。该报告强烈暗示这是一件回收的人工制造装置或部件，而非不明飞行器，但该文件并未记载最终的技术鉴定。

001_1947-07-07_West Rindge, Rindge, New.report_summary:
**Document:** FBI Communications Section teletype, Washington from Boston 3, dated Jul. 18, 1947, in file 62-HQ-83894. The page is marked “Security Matter-X” and records a post-incident inquiry rather than a direct field report. It is stamped as page one, with “End page one” at the bottom; no continuation page was provided in this extract.

**Witness:** Dean John M. Bunker, security officer at M.I.T., Cambridge, informed the FBI that he had spoken with Charles N. Tasker of West Rindge, New Hampshire, a retired vice president of the New England Telephone and Telegraph Company. Tasker was the relaying source for the original observation made by several unnamed people seated on a porch near the scene.

**Sighting:** Around 3:00 PM on July 7, 1947, observers on a porch saw little curls of smoke on the lawn of Earl Whitehead, Route 2, West Rindge. On inspection, they found small burned spots about 1.5 inches in diameter on the green lawn and additional small blazes in long, dry grass on both sides of the road, within a roughly 200-foot-diameter area. The fire department was called.

**Object/Material:** The fires were reportedly caused by “metallic fragmentations” turned over to Professor Rentges of M.I.T. by Parke D. Appel of the telephone company. Rentges told Bunker the fragments’ general appearance resembled the lining of V-2 bombs he had seen in New Mexico. Another M.I.T. metallurgist, Professor L.H. Newald, suggested they might be from a jet turbo plane. He was analyzing two pieces at the time of the report. The scientists’ rough reconstruction indicated a metallic object approximately 14 inches in diameter. The page does not identify a flying disc, but instead describes debris analysis and possible mundane military/aircraft origins.
001_1947-07-07_West Rindge, Rindge, New.report_summary_zh:
**Document:** FBI 通讯科电传，华盛顿发自波士顿 3，日期为 1947年7月18日，存于档案 62-HQ-83894。该页标注为“Security Matter-X”，记录的是事后调查而非直接的现场报告。页面上盖有“page one”字样，底部注明“End page one”；在此摘录中未提供后续页面。

**Witness:** M.I.T.（麻省理工学院）剑桥校区的保安官 Dean John M. Bunker 告知 FBI，他曾与来自新罕布什尔州 West Rindge 的 Charles N. Tasker 谈过话；Tasker 是 New England Telephone and Telegraph Company（新英格兰电话电报公司）的退休副总裁。Tasker 是转述最初目击情况的人，而最初的观察来自几名坐在事发地点附近门廊上的未署名人士。

**Sighting:** 1947年7月7日约下午 3:00，门廊上的目击者在 Earl Whitehead 位于 Route 2, West Rindge 的草坪上看到了少量烟圈。经查看，他们发现绿色草坪上有直径约 1.5 英寸的小烧灼痕，路两侧的长而干燥的草丛中还有更多小火点，范围大约在直径 200 英尺的区域内。随后有人呼叫了消防部门。

**Object/Material:** 据称，这些火是由“metallic fragmentations”引起的，这些碎片由电话公司员工 Parke D. Appel 交给了 M.I.T. 的 Rentges 教授。Rentges 告诉 Bunker，这些碎片的外观大致类似于他在 New Mexico 见过的 V-2 炸弹内衬。M.I.T. 另一位冶金学家、L.H. Newald 教授则认为它们可能来自喷气式涡轮飞机。报告成文时，他正在分析其中两块碎片。科学家的粗略推断表明，这是一件直径约 14 英寸的金属物体。该页并未提及飞碟，而是描述了碎片分析以及可能的普通军事/航空器来源。

001_1947-07-15_Seattle, Washington (2608.report_summary:
**Document:** FBI Seattle sent an urgent teletype to the Director, Communications Section, dated Jul. 16, 1947 at 10:15 AM, under the broader UFO/flying-disc file. The report is a field-originated summary rather than a formal investigative memo, and it records immediate Bureau response and follow-up examination.

**Witness:** Mrs. T. L. Kremmer, identified with an address at 2608 Third Ave. West, Seattle, reported the incident to authorities. The page does not provide a long biographical profile, but her position at the location and the prompt FBI response suggest she was an on-scene civilian observer/occupant rather than a distant hearsay source.

**Sighting:** She said that about 9:42 PM the previous night, a “flying disk” had landed on the roof near her offices and was burning when noticed; it was immediately extinguished. The wording is messy in places, but the core report is of a small object found on/near the roof of the office building, not a distant aerial sighting.

**Object:** Agents were dispatched immediately and recovered the item. Navy bomb and electronics experts, along with FBI agents, examined it. The object was described as a roughly 28-inch circular piece of 3/16-inch plywood cupped on two sides and held by wire across its center, painted light gray outside and red inside. Inside were white-painted markings reading “U S S R” and “E Y R” (apparently “RYE” backward), plus a hammer and sickle. It also contained two radio tubes, an oil can, rubber tubing, a one-inch pipe, and a cloth plug with charred ends.

**Investigation / conclusion:** The physical description strongly suggests a crude homemade or planted device rather than an aircraft or unknown vehicle. The report shows the FBI taking the event seriously enough to dispatch agents and technical experts, but the recovered item’s construction is consistent with a hoax, propaganda device, or odd mechanical assemblage rather than a genuine flying disk.
001_1947-07-15_Seattle, Washington (2608.report_summary_zh:

**Witness:** T. L. Kremmer夫人，登记地址为2608 Third Ave. West, Seattle，向当局报告了这一事件。页面未提供详细的个人背景资料，但她所在位置以及FBI的迅速反应表明，她是一名在现场的平民目击者/占有人，而非远距离的转述消息来源。

**Sighting:** 她称在前一晚约9:42 PM，一块“飞碟”落在她办公室附近的屋顶上，被发现时正在燃烧；随即被扑灭。措辞在某些地方较为混乱，但核心内容是：在办公楼屋顶上或附近发现了一件小物体，而非远距离的空中目击。

001_1947-06-21_Maury Island (Puget Sound.report_summary:
**Document:** FBI Seattle teletype to the Director in case file 62-HQ-83894, Section 1, dated **AUG 14 1947, 5:15 PM**, marked “ROUTINE” and signed/initialed “WILCOX.” The message is a short intelligence-style follow-up on the Tacoma-area “flying discs” story and notes that the complete report was still en route to Bureau HQ. The page carries standard FBI communications-section stamping and later indexing/recording marks.

**Witness:** The report concerns **Harold A. Dahl** and **Fred Chrisman**, both treated here as civilian witnesses. The Seattle office relays that Dahl did not directly tell “Smith” the story was a hoax, but said that if authorities questioned him he would describe it as a hoax because he wanted no further trouble. That statement, plus the surrounding context, is used by the Bureau to question the credibility of the account.

**Sighting:** The teletype summarizes a “flying discs” sighting in the **Tacoma / Puget Sound area** associated with Chrisman and Dahl. The page itself does not give the full narrative of the observation, but it clearly identifies the incident as the one later known as the Maury Island story. The underlying sighting date is taken as **21 Jun 1947**.

**Object:** The objects are described only generically as “flying discs.” No dimensions, color, number, maneuvering details, or flight path are provided on this page.

**Investigation:** FBI Seattle concludes the anonymous phone call was probably made by Chrisman or Dahl in an effort to build publicity and possibly secure a profitable deal with **Fantasy Magazine, Chicago, Illinois**. The teletype says Dahl and Chrisman would not be reinterviewed unless the Bureau advised otherwise, indicating the Bureau viewed the matter skeptically and suspected a hoax/publicity scheme rather than a reliable UFO report.
001_1947-06-21_Maury Island (Puget Sound.report_summary_zh:
**Document:** FBI西雅图分局致局长的电传，案卷号62-HQ-83894，第1节，日期为**1947年8月14日，下午5:15**，标记为“ROUTINE”，并由“WILCOX”签署/首字母签注。该电报是一则简短的情报式后续报告，涉及塔科马地区“飞碟”事件，并指出完整报告仍在送往局总部的途中。该页带有标准的FBI通信科盖章，以及后来的索引/登记标记。

**Witness:** 报告涉及**Harold A. Dahl**和**Fred Chrisman**，在此均作为平民目击者对待。西雅图办公室转述说，Dahl并未直接告诉“Smith”这起事件是骗局，但表示如果当局询问他，他会把它描述成骗局，因为他不想再惹麻烦。FBI据此加上周边情境，对该说法的可信度提出质疑。

**Sighting:** 这份电传概述了发生在**Tacoma / Puget Sound area**、与Chrisman和Dahl有关的一次“飞碟”目击事件。页面本身并未给出完整的观察叙述，但明确将该事件识别为后来所称的Maury Island事件。其基础目击日期定为**1947年6月21日**。

**Object:** 这些物体仅被笼统描述为“flying discs（飞碟）”。本页未提供尺寸、颜色、数量、机动细节或飞行轨迹。

**Investigation:** FBI西雅图分局认定，这通匿名电话很可能是Chrisman或Dahl打来的，意在制造宣传，并可能与**Fantasy Magazine, Chicago, Illinois**达成一笔有利可图的交易。电传称，除非局方另有建议，否则不会再次对Dahl和Chrisman进行访谈，这表明FBI对该事持怀疑态度，认为其更可能是骗局/炒作方案，而非可信的UFO报告。

001_1947-08-03_Hackensack, Bergen County.report_summary:
**Document:** Single-page FBI teletype in file **62-HQ-83894, Section 1**. Header reads **“WASHINGTON 1 FROM NEWARK”** and is dated **AUG. 4, 1947, 5:36 PM EDST**; the page is marked **“DIRECTOR URGENT”** and signed/initialed **McKee**. It is a Communications Section transmission reporting a UFO-related sighting and noting that inquiry was underway. No later page in the provided sequence appears to continue this same incident.

**Witness:** The report names **Charles Casella, Jr.**, age 20, of **28 Euclid Avenue, Hackensack**, as the principal observer. It also identifies **William Truex, U.S. Army, Ft. Dix, NJ** as another person who saw the object from the ground on the same occasion. Casella is described as having telephoned the information to the Hackensack Police Department.

**Sighting:** The event is dated to the **late afternoon of August 3, 1947** in **Hackensack, New Jersey**. The object was described as a **“flying disc”** seen from the ground and reportedly at about **200 yards** distance. Casella said it was **in the air**, **revolving slowly**, and **moving rapidly**, and emphasized that it was **neither a kite nor a balloon**. The teletype does not record duration, altitude estimate beyond the 200-yard figure, weather, or any physical effects.

**Investigation:** FBI Newark forwarded the report to FBI headquarters as urgent miscellaneous information. The page states only that **inquiry [was] being made** and that the **Bureau will be kept advised**. No identification or explanation is reached on this page. As a contemporaneous law-enforcement relay of a civilian sighting, the file preserves a first-hand claim but provides no corroborating evidence, making it an unverified visual report rather than a solved case.
001_1947-08-03_Hackensack, Bergen County.report_summary_zh:
**Document:** 文件中的单页 FBI 电传稿，见 **62-HQ-83894, Section 1**。页眉写着 **“WASHINGTON 1 FROM NEWARK”**，日期为 **AUG. 4, 1947, 5:36 PM EDST**；页面标注 **“DIRECTOR URGENT”**，并由 **McKee** 签名/首字母缩写。该页为通信科传输件，报告了一起与 UFO 相关的目击事件，并注明调查正在进行中。所提供的序列中没有后续页面显示这一同一事件的继续。

001_1967-10-09_Dallas, Texas (Dallas FBI.report_summary:
**Document:** FBI Dallas memorandum on U.S. Department of Justice/Federal Bureau of Investigation letterhead, dated October 10, 1967, file reference 62-HQ-83894 (Section 10). The subject line reads “Unidentified Flying Objects; Anonymous Informant; Dallas, Texas; October 9, 1967.” The page includes the standard FBI disclaimer that it contains no recommendations or conclusions and is loaned to another agency.

**Witness:** A young white female, who refused to give her name, appeared at the Dallas FBI Office on October 9, 1967. She said she was interested in UFOs and had received a quantity of information about beings from outer space. She would not reveal her identity, saying she would feel foolish if the information proved untrue, but said she would cooperate further if officials were interested and could ensure her safety.

**Sighting / Claim:** This was not a direct visual sighting report by the witness; it was an anonymous tip containing alleged extraterrestrial contact and second-hand “messages.” She claimed that in July 1967 she met a being from another planet who had assumed earthly form, gave her information, was later “picked up,” and departed Earth on August 21, 1967. She then reportedly received further messages from non-earthly sources, which she would not discuss.

**Object / Allegations:** The information passed to the FBI included four claims: an antimissile missile fired at a UFO over Africa on May 22, 1962, but the craft was protected by a “force field”; a UFO detected 22,000 miles from Earth by radar about August 6, 1967; a UFO detected over Antarctica on August 20, 1967; and a UFO detected over the “Dewline” in the previous week, shot down, with beings from outer space trying to recover it. No corroborating evidence, names, or technical details were provided.

**Investigation:** The memorandum records the informant’s statements only; it does not describe any FBI validation, recommendation, or conclusion. The file is best understood as an intake/reporting document, not an authenticated UFO incident.

001_1974-08-21_Milwaukee, Wisconsin (rec.report_summary:
**Document:** FBI Headquarters memorandum on Optional Form No. 10, from T. J. Smith to W. R. Wannall, dated 8/22/74, under file 62-HQ-83894 / REC-101, subject “Military inquiry regarding unidentified object that fell from sky at Milwaukee, Wisconsin, 8/21/74; information concerning.” The page shows routing and initials from FBI offices and staff, indicating internal distribution rather than a field interview report.

**Incident:** At 12:07 a.m. on 8/22/74, Security Patrol Clerk Charles F. Halty of the FBI Intelligence Division received a call through the Command Center from Maj. Horn of NMMC (National Military Command Center). Horn asked whether the FBI had information on a report that an unidentified object had fallen from the sky at Milwaukee and had been recovered by local police and turned over to the Milwaukee FBI Office. A later call to Night Duty Supervisor Harry E. Morris, Jr., confirmed that Milwaukee police had recovered the object at about 5:55 p.m. on 8/21/74 and still possessed it. Capt. Wills of the Milwaukee Police Department had reportedly called the Milwaukee FBI Office about the recovery.

**Object:** The object was described only as about 13 x 8 x 5 inches, metallic in substance and color, jagged on one side, and having an “internal heat source.” No direct eyewitness to the fall is identified in this memo, and the FBI states that very little was known about the object. Police notified military authorities locally.

**Investigation:** The information was relayed back to Maj. Horn with the suggestion that he contact Capt. Wills. The memo notes that the matter received United Press International coverage the morning of 8/22/74. The FBI action was simply “For information,” with no analytical conclusion beyond the limited descriptive facts and the fact of recovery by police.

001_1949-07-01_Lake of the Woods (vicini.report_summary:
**Document:** FBI Office Memorandum, Standard Form No. 64, dated September 6, 1949, from SAC Indianapolis to the Director, FBI, subject “Flying Saucers / Security Matter - X.” The page bears recorded/indexed stamps for file 62-HQ-83894 and is presented as information only; the memo ends by saying the Bureau is taking no action.

**Witness / source chain:** The memo was written after Elbert W. Farris of the OSI at Benjamin Harrison Air Base contacted the Indianapolis FBI office seeking current information on “flying saucers.” Farris said he had been directed to contact Dr. Richard K. Parrish of Decatur, Indiana, who allegedly observed a saucer. The report also mentions an FBI Agent Metcalf of the Omaha office, who was said to have seen the same object.

**Sighting:** Parrish’s alleged observation is placed in the vicinity of Lake of the Woods, Canada, on or about July 1, 1949. The memo does not give a precise time, altitude, direction, size, lights, sound, or flight behavior; the object is referred to only generically as a “flying saucer.”

**Object / interpretation:** The page focuses less on the craft itself than on Parrish’s later interpretation. Farris reported that Parrish believed some Decatur, Indiana polio cases were not polio but possibly uranium poisoning, and that the presence of flying saucers had a bearing on the epidemic. Parrish also cited earlier saucer sightings in the Carolinas in 1948 alongside a polio outbreak there.

**Investigation / disposition:** Farris said he had consulted a physician at Benjamin Harrison Air Base, checked records concerning saucer allegations, and had done research on any correlation between saucer reports and polio outbreaks. He also said he was reporting the matter to Air Force authorities at Wright Field. The memo further notes that Indiana University Medical School personnel treated the matter as a joke. The FBI forwarded the information for Bureau awareness only and did not open action on the matter.

001_1949-05-27_near Burns, Oregon (Harne.report_summary:
**Document:** Confidential intelligence report DIO-11ND Serial 32-49, issued by the Intelligence Division, Office of Chief of Naval Operations, Navy Department, dated 23 June 1949, preserved in FBI case file 62-HQ-83894 Section 5. Page 1 is a cover sheet with source biography; page 2 contains the narrative report titled "Unidentified Flying Objects Observed in Oregon 27 May 1949."

**Witness:** The source is identified as Joseph C. Shell, USNR (Inactive), a former naval aviator, commercial pilot, flight instructor, and vice-president of the Royal Petroleum Company of California. The report notes a Naval Aviator Certificate, multiple pilot/instructor ratings, and roughly 5,300 total flight hours, which the writer treats as supporting his reliability as an observer.

**Sighting:** On 27 May 1949, about 2:25 p.m. PST, Shell was flying his own SNJ-type aircraft toward Burns, Oregon. He first noticed sunlight glinting off an object ahead and to his left, then realized it was not one object but about six or seven separate objects. The report places the observation over the southern Oregon area near Burns, including the Harney Mountain / dry-lake region, while the objects moved roughly parallel to his course.

**Object:** Shell described the objects as solid, elongated ovals or egg-shaped forms, apparently smaller than a fighter and probably under 20 feet long. He reported no visible wings, fuselage break, exhaust, smoke, or other trail; the objects appeared to be metallic and unpainted. He estimated they were several miles away, 2,000-2,500 feet below his altitude, and moving at roughly 190-260 mph, likely above 230 mph.

**Investigation:** The report relies on a single, technically qualified witness and gives no corroborating observers. The Navy intelligence author did not identify the objects as conventional aircraft and left them classified as unidentified flying objects.

**Document:** These three consecutive pages form one FBI/UFO correspondence chain around the same sighting. Page 0039 is a Standard Form 64 office memorandum from the SAC, Pittsburgh to the Director, FBI, dated October 2, 1949, forwarding the attached letter from Glen Sprouse. Page 0040 is Sprouse’s original letter to the FBI, dated September 25, 1949. Page 0041 is a Headquarters memorandum from J. Edgar Hoover to the Air Force Inspector General, dated October 19, 1949, summarizing the same report as unverified information from a confidential source. File markings include 62-HQ-83894-202 and exhibit tags EX-119/EX-119A.

**Witness:** Glen Sprouse of 608 Montrose Drive, S. Charleston, West Virginia, reported the event after voluntarily appearing at the Charleston resident agency and turning over his letter to Special Agent John B. Woodruff. He stated he was the pilot of a Luscombe 8A (NC 1440K) and was flying with his wife, who did not see the object.

**Sighting:** On September 25, 1949, at about 2:45 P.M., while flying from Clark Field, St. Albans, to Parkersburg, Sprouse said that roughly four miles southwest of Parkersburg, over a dark green wooded background, he suddenly saw a bright yellow object moving directly toward him. It passed in a few seconds about 100 feet below his aircraft and about 50 feet to the right.

**Object:** Sprouse described a bright canary-yellow body, about 15 to 18 inches long and roughly 4 inches in diameter at its widest point. He said it looked like a rocket, with the same general proportions as the fuselage of a Lockheed Air Force X-90, but with no wings and with vertical and horizontal fins near the rear third. He reported a very sharp needle nose, a blunt tail, and no visible propulsion, smoke, vapor trail, or exhaust. He believed it was not a mirage and said it appeared to be dropping slightly as it passed.

**Investigation:** The FBI recorded the report but took no further action unless directed. Hoover’s later memo repeated that the information was unverified and came from a source whose reliability was unknown. The file preserves the sighting as a daylight, close-range, pilot-observed UFO report, but no identification or explanation was reached.

001_1950-03-09_Denver University (Denver.report_summary:
**Document:** FBI Denver sent an urgent teletype to the Director, FBI, at 9:25 PM on 9 Mar 1950 in case file 62-HQ-83894, Section 5. The page is marked with internal routing/approval initials and signed "Kramer." It reads like an intelligence lead rather than a formal field report.

**Witness:** No direct eyewitness is named. The report says two sources advised the Bureau that an unidentified man had given at least one, and possibly more, lectures before classes at Denver University. The man reportedly refused to reveal his identity, but was known to George Koehler, who was connected with radio station KMYR, Denver.

**Sighting:** The lecturer allegedly said he had personally observed flying saucers. He claimed to have seen several such objects, one of which allegedly landed in New Mexico. He also claimed to have observed occupants of the saucers, describing them as human in form but about three feet tall, and said these occupants were dead when he saw them.

**Investigation:** The FBI note says local press and wire services were already carrying stories about the Denver University lectures. OSI Denver reported no additional information, except that Koehler had made similar claims in January and, after investigation, had been unable to produce verifiable information. OSI considered Koehler a probable mental case. The page contains no corroborated physical evidence and no confirmed identity for the lecturer; it is best read as a report of sensational UFO claims circulating through local media and informants, not as a validated sighting.

001_1950-01-25_Paxinos, Pennsylvania (fr.report_summary:
**Document:** Handwritten civilian letter dated “Paxinos Pa Feb 14th 1950,” preserved in FBI file 62-HQ-83894, Section 5. The page bears FBI receipt/recording stamps from late February 1950. No classification marking or formal investigative report text is visible on this page.

Entries give times and directions from the home rather than detailed visual descriptions: Jan. 25 at 10:15 a.m. southeast, 3:00 p.m. southwest, and 4:00 p.m.; Jan. 26 from 11:30 a.m. to 12:30 p.m. south or east; Jan. 27 at noon and later times, apparently toward the south/southwest/east; Jan. 28 at 11:00 a.m. east; Jan. 29 at 1:00 p.m. and also at night; Jan. 30 at 2:00 p.m. northwest; Feb. 3 at 10:00 a.m., 11:00 a.m., and noon southeast; Feb. 4 at 11:30 a.m. and 2:30 p.m. southwest; Feb. 8 from about 11:45 a.m. to 12:15 p.m. and 1:30-2:05 p.m. west; and Feb. 10 at night, about 8:40 p.m., west.

**Object:** The writer repeatedly uses “flying discs” or “flying saucers,” but gives no reliable shape, size, color, altitude, speed, sound, duration, or maneuver details beyond date, time, and direction.

**Investigation:** The page is best treated as an uncorroborated citizen data submission asking the FBI to compare the dates with other saucer reports. No follow-up finding, witness interview, or Project Saucer/Air Force conclusion appears on this page.

The page is marked confidential/classified-style and appears to be an analytical summary rather than a first-person narrative. No signer is visible on this page.

**Witness:** The source is an experienced aircraft pilot who regularly flew between California and Oregon. The memo treats him as a credible observer: he knew the valley route, could estimate altitudes, and was familiar with the terrain and traffic patterns. He reported that he had not seen other aircraft in the valley on prior flights and believed the area was sparsely populated but not empty.

**Sighting:** The objects were seen over a north-south valley in south-central Oregon, described as about 12 miles wide with a floor around 4,000–5,000 feet MSL and the east side dominated by Hart Mountain / a dark bluff. The source was flying north while the objects moved south. From an estimated 9,000-foot aircraft altitude, the objects were judged to be roughly in line with the 7,000-foot rim of the bluff and probably around 8,000 feet MSL, or about 3,500 feet above the valley floor. Visibility was said to be exceptionally good, with scattered clouds high overhead and only light haze.

**Object:** At first the witness could not separate the lights/reflections, but as he closed to within about 5–7 miles he distinctly saw 5 to 8 separate objects, probably 6 or 7. They were always in single-file formation with very constant spacing, showing no obvious change in relative altitude. The memo says they appeared metallic or “unpainted metal,” stood out sharply against the dark terrain, and were rigidly grouped; terrain could reportedly be seen between them. The analyst noted the formation’s spacing and motion suggested multiple separate craft rather than a single object.

**Investigation:** The report notes the valley is sparsely populated, with ranches that might yield ground witnesses, but it is not a commercial airline route and is seldom used by private aircraft. The page offers no final identification or explanation.

He said it moved from northwest to southeast at an excessive speed, nearly overhead, at an estimated altitude of 15,000 to 20,000 feet, and stayed visible for about 20 to 25 seconds before disappearing over the horizon.

**Object:** The informant described the object as about five feet long in appearance from his viewpoint, with the front two-thirds glowing like a burning kerosene lamp and the rear third dark. It left a bluish-white trail about four inches wide and roughly three times the object's length. He reported no visible wings or support structure, no discernible sound, and unknown propulsion, control, and stability. He said it did not resemble a falling star or meteor, though it was much faster than any conventional aircraft he had seen.

**Investigation:** The memo states there were no other witnesses. The report is forwarded to the Bureau “for whatever action it may deem advisable,” and no analytical conclusion is offered beyond the field office’s characterization of the informant and observations.

001_1950-07-04_Alice Municipal Airport a.report_summary:
**Document:** FBI Houston teletype(s) to the Director in the Communications Section, file 62-HQ-83894 (Section 5), dated July 4, 1950. The first transmission at 2:35 PM CST reported a “flying disc” said to have been found near Alice, Texas, and noted a reported serial number “X-147A” plus instructions quoted as “do not touch.” A second Houston teletype at 3:50 PM CST follows up with the result of the inquiry.

**Witness:** The principal local source named in the follow-up is Stokes McEnheimer, Chief of Police, Alice, Texas. The report also notes that a resident agent in Corpus Christi had heard local radio commentary suggesting the discovery was a hoax.

**Sighting:** The object was said to have been found on July 4, 1950, in a field about 100 yards northwest of the municipal airport at Alice. Initial descriptions characterized it as a small, elliptical contraption about five feet in diameter, freshly painted, and bearing the markings mentioned in the first teletype.

**Investigation:** McEnheimer advised that the object was built by welding together portions of two airplane wings. It had no motor or means of propulsion, and after examination the police concluded it had been constructed by a group of mechanics at the Alice airport as a practical joke. Air Force officials at Ellington Field were notified, and the Bureau closed the matter with no further inquiry. The page set documents a quickly resolved flying-disc hoax rather than a genuine unexplained aerial incident.

No official conclusion is stated on this page, but the report notes that military officers at **Godman Field** were notified and flight headquarters at **Wright-Patterson Field** were informed. The memo preserves the incident as a contemporaneous press-and-bureau summary of a photographed UFO sighting rather than a completed investigation.

001_1950-01-22_Kodiak Naval Air Station.report_summary:
**Document:** Confidential memo, DIC/17TD No. 4-50, dated 10 February 1950, subject “Unidentified Phenomena.” The page is numbered 2 and summarizes information from enclosures (1) through (8). It appears in FBI case-file material but describes Navy-origin reports from the Kodiak, Alaska area.

**Witnesses:** The primary witness is Lt. L. T. Smith, USN, patrol plane commander of PV/PBY patrol aircraft with Patrol Squadron One. Additional observers include radar operator G. Skeen, USN; Morgan, FTC, USN aboard USS *Tilamook* (ATA-192); Carver, CN, USN; and later Lt. Causer, Lt. Parco, and plane captain Paulson.

**Sighting:** The page describes several related events around Kodiak on 22-23 January 1950. Smith first reported an unidentified radar contact about 20 miles north of NAS Kodiak, then another contact about 10 miles southeast of the station. During the same period he was also involved in a visual/radar encounter in which an object appeared on the radar scope at about 5 miles, then came directly overhead, reportedly suggesting very high speed. He estimated roughly 1,800 mph and said the object maneuvered too quickly for him to intercept or circle.

**Object:** Descriptions vary by observer but include a very fast-moving red light, a “ball of fire” about one foot in diameter, a blip with a tail-like indication on radar, and an airborne object that seemed to open out, turn left, and come up on the aircraft’s quarter. No sound was detected in the shipboard sighting. The object later departed to the southeast. Another patrol the following day reportedly saw an unidentified object on an ascending westerly course for about ten minutes, but could not close with it at 170 knots.

**Assessment:** The report reflects trained military observers, multiple corroborating sightings, and at least some radar involvement, but the page offers no identification or firm conclusion. The observations are brief, inconsistent in appearance, and partly dependent on radar interpretation; the document itself frames them as unexplained phenomena rather than a solved incident.
001_1950-01-22_Kodiak Naval Air Station.report_summary_zh:
**Document:** 机密备忘录，DIC/17TD No. 4-50，日期为 1950年2月10日，主题为“Unidentified Phenomena.”。该页编号为 2，并汇总了附件（1）至（8）中的信息。其出现在 FBI 案卷材料中，但所述内容为来自 Alaska(阿拉斯加) Kodiak(科迪亚克) 地区的海军报告。

**Witnesses:** 主要目击者为 Lt. L. T. Smith, USN，Patrol Squadron One 的 PV/PBY 巡逻机机长。其他观察者包括雷达操作员 G. Skeen, USN；USS *Tilamook* (ATA-192) 舰上的 Morgan, FTC, USN；Carver, CN, USN；以及后来的 Lt. Causer、Lt. Parco 和机长 Paulson。

001_1950-09-26_Philadelphia, Pennsylvani.report_summary:
**Document:** FBI Office Memorandum (Standard Form No. 64), dated October 2, 1950, from the SAC, Philadelphia, to the Director, FBI, attention Mr. Leo Laughlin. Subject line: “Flying Disc Reported at Philadelphia on 9/26/50.” The page carries FBI routing and later handling marks, including a note that the matter was referred to Air Force Intelligence and then to OSI, with no further FBI action taken.

**Witness:** The report is based on two Philadelphia police officers on duty, described as observing the incident firsthand in the late evening hours of September 26, 1950. No individual names are given in this memo, so the witness set is limited to their official role and agency.

**Sighting:** While on Vare Boulevard near 26th Street in Philadelphia, the officers saw a round object about six feet in circumference slowly float down to the ground. It reportedly had the appearance of a parachute and came to rest in a field without depressing the weeds, suggesting it was extremely light. The object was described as lavender in color and “dewy,” “sort of like soap suds,” and it evaporated within 15 to 20 minutes after landing. When touched by the officers, the substance disappeared, leaving only a slight sticky residue.

**Assessment / provenance:** The memo states the report was made to the FBI by the Philadelphia Police and later appeared in the Philadelphia press under the headline “Flying Saucer Just Dissolves.” The language of the report strongly suggests a transient foam-like or soap-suds-like material rather than a conventional metallic craft, and the memo records no definitive identification. The FBI treated it as a field report to be passed to Air Force Intelligence, not as an active FBI investigation.

001_1952-03-06_Chicago, Illinois (over F.report_summary:
**Document:** FBI Office Memorandum No. 64, from the SAC, Chicago (file 100-18999) to the Director, FBI (62-83894), dated March 21, 1952, subject “Flying Discs – Karl Nyquist, Informant.” The page is stamped declassified and bears routing/record stamps showing it was recorded and indexed in the Bureau’s files. The memorandum was written by SA Myron H. Treter (MHT:BJB) after speaking with the witness and forwarding the report and sketch to the local Office of Special Investigations.

**Witness:** Karl Nyquist, identified as an artist living at 2417 North Burling Street, Chicago, Illinois, told SA Treter on March 11, 1952 about a sighting he said occurred at 9:00 AM on March 6, 1952. He is described as a civilian informant, not a trained observer, but he gave a detailed narrative and produced a sketch.

**Sighting:** Nyquist said he was looking south from a window in his home when he saw a flying disc approximately 7,000 feet above Fullerton Avenue, with an elevation angle of about 45 degrees. He reported the object emerged from a cloud in the east, paused motionless for a split second, then flew due south at great speed and vanished in about three seconds. He estimated the speed at 600–700 mph or more.

**Object:** The disc was described as circular, about six feet in diameter, white with a bluish tinge, and appearing to be made of a metal similar to aluminum. Nyquist reported no exhaust, no lights, and no sound. He also said nothing was visible to explain how it maintained flight and believed it may have been radio controlled. When it disappeared, he said it was about the size of a golf ball on the southern horizon.

**Investigation:** The memo preserves the report as received; it does not record a Bureau conclusion, but it notes that Nyquist’s sketch and information were furnished to the local Office of Special Investigations.

**Object:** 他将这些飞行器形容为“saucer-like discs”，并认为除非物体处于很高的高度，否则地面观察者很难做出准确描述。他指出，地面附近的空气湿度和尘埃可能会扭曲视觉，而空中观察者则会更准确。这与经典的 flying-disc 描述一致，而不是对常规飞机的辨认。

**Investigation/Context:** Arnold 引用了美国各地多名观察者据称相似的报告，包括 Utah 的 Cedar City 的 Western Air Lines 员工；来自 Oklahoma City 的一名飞行员；Illinois 的一名机车工程师；Boise 的 United Press 的 John Corlett；Boise Daily Statesman 的 Dave Johnson；以及 United Air Lines 的人员 Captain Smith、co-pilot Stevens、Marty Morrow、Captain Charles F. Gabian 和 Jack Harvey。他还说自己收到了来自美国和欧洲的来信。该页的分析重点在于，许多目击可能属于同一种现象，但并未作出明确鉴定。

001_1947-08-06_Philadelphia, Pennsylvani.report_summary:
**Document:** FBI Office Memorandum (Standard Form No. 64) from SAC, Philadelphia, to the Director, FBI, dated September 18, 1947. Subject line: "Flying object reported over Philadelphia August 6, 1947" with "sabotage" typed beneath. This page appears to be the complete visible report excerpt for the incident; no continuation page is shown. The file context is FBI case file 62-HQ-83894, Section 3, and the page bears later indexing/recording stamps and marginal handwritten notes typical of UFO-era file handling.

**Witness:** The first and primary account is from Miss Eleanor Naddle, 2114 Hobart Street, Philadelphia, employed by the George R. Greenwald Manufacturing Company. Secondary corroborating statements follow from Miss Cecelia Fine, 5617 Arlington Street, employed by Pressman & Gutman Company, Inc., and John Snyder, 1440 Vankirk Street, an insurance agent and former B-24 pilot in the Army Air Corps.

**Sighting:** Naddle said that between 10:30 and 10:45 p.m. on August 6, 1947, while sitting on her front steps with Fine, she saw a large white object moving very fast to the south. She reported a buzzing sound and a thin grayish smoke trail. Fine said she did not actually see the object, but noticed Naddle become frightened and heard a slight buzzing sound.

**Object:** Snyder, viewing the same general event around 10:45 p.m. with his wife and neighbors, described a bluish-white flame or object traveling quickly from northeast to southwest. Using his aviation experience, he estimated it at 1,000-3,000 feet altitude and 400-500 mph, leaving smoke or a condensation trail for about two seconds and making a hissing sound less loud than a rocket ship.

**Investigation:** The memorandum is a straight factual relay from the Philadelphia field office; no identification or final explanation is stated on this page. The combined descriptions emphasize a fast-moving luminous object with sound and a short-lived trail, but the record here stops short of concluding what it was.

The object was visible for about 15–20 seconds, traveling due south and apparently below scattered clouds that were reported above 10,000 feet.

**Investigation:** The FBI report records the observations without drawing a firm conclusion. The object’s speed was described as greater than any plane seen by the witnesses, but the narrative offers no identification, only the eyewitness characteristics and the conflicting size estimates.

001_1947-05-05_Ellensburg–Seattle corrid.report_summary:
**Document:** FBI Office Memorandum, sent from the Butte field office to the Director, FBI, dated September 27, 1947, in file 62-HQ-83894, Section 3. The page is an internal UFO/flying-disc report with routing references to Seattle and the 4th Air Force (S-2, McChord Field). It carries Bureau notation, file stamps, and initials indicating internal review and indexing.

**Witness:** The report centers on Warden John Henry of Montana State Prison, Deer Lodge, Montana, who relayed the account to the FBI writer. His account was corroborated by Melbourne M. Hill, identified as a convict chauffeur, and Mrs. Henry. The memorandum notes that Henry delayed reporting because he had already seen extensive newspaper coverage of the disc stories and initially thought the matter might be dismissed as "seeing things."

**Sighting:** On May 5, 1947, at about 3:30 P.M., while driving between Ellensburg and Seattle, Washington, Henry and the two other observers saw a silver object streak across the sky. He said it entered a nose dive and appeared likely to crash, but before reaching the earth it disintegrated, leaving a long smoky or gaseous pillar hanging high in the air. The object reportedly retained its form until breakup and did not blow away immediately.

**Object:** Henry described the target as moving at an extremely high speed with erratic motion at first, causing him to think it might be a jet-propelled plane, though he could not identify it. The memo emphasizes that the smoky pillar remained suspended and that the object was still far from the ground when it came apart.

**Investigation:** The Butte office concluded no further action was warranted because of the delay between the sighting and the report. The Seattle office was asked to advise H. R. Peterson of the 4th Air Force, but the case file page itself presents no technical analysis or identification beyond the witness descriptions.

001_1947-08-12_Boeing Field, Seattle, Wa.report_summary:
**Document:** FBI Seattle SAC memorandum to the Director, dated Sept. 12, 1947, in file 62-HQ-83894, “Security Matter X,” subject “FLYING DISKS Reported by BRUCE ARMSTRONG and M. A. NICHOLS, Seattle, Washington, August 12, 1947.” The second page is a direct continuation of the same report (header “FLYING DISKS, Report of 8/26/47”), so both rendered pages belong to one case file item.

**Witness:** The primary witness was Bruce Armstrong, identified as an electronics technician at the Boeing Aircraft plant. The report also names M. A. Nichols of Seattle as a second sighting witness, with additional corroboration from Ray Stanley, George and Mrs. Krogstad, and Boeing Field personnel.

**Sighting:** Armstrong stated that about 2:20 p.m. on August 12, 1947, while standing in front of Section D of the Boeing Aircraft Plant with about ten other research engineers, he saw a small black object about 200 feet high moving south over the Boeing Field runway. He described it as triangular, fluttering “like a leaf,” and estimated its speed at about 15 mph. The engineers’ consensus was that it resembled a black leaf or tar paper. Later, report text notes another sighting by Nichols at about 4 p.m., who said he saw an object over his home moving southwest at a much higher altitude, with observers describing it as a white, cylindrical object reflecting sunlight with a purplish tinge.

**Investigation:** The Seattle office interviewed control-tower operator Ken Grant and Boeing Field weather-bureau personnel. Grant suggested the low object may have been a piece of burnt paper blown across the field; weather personnel noted that balloons were released every six hours from Boeing Field, were white in color, and could reflect sunlight at altitude. The report concludes that the observed object was probably a balloon or other debris and states that no further investigation would be conducted.
001_1947-08-12_Boeing Field, Seattle, Wa.report_summary_zh:

001_1949-04-05_Logan, Utah (west of town.report_summary:
**Document:** FBI Salt Lake City sent an urgent Communications Section teletype to the Director on 5 Apr 1949, stamped "FBI SALT LAKE CITY" and "TELETYPE," with later routing/handling marks and the file context of FBI case 62-HQ-83894, Section 4. The page is a single-page report (p.0126) and appears to be the primary record for this incident.

**Witness:** The initial account was relayed from Logan, Utah, based on what an unnamed guard at the Army General Supply Depot in Ogden said he saw at about 9:00 AM. Additional contemporaneous observers included Lt. Ron Hatfield of the Logan Police Department, Utah Highway Patrolman L. N. Jeppson at Mantua, and several residents at Trenton. Because the report is a teletype summary rather than a signed field interview, the first-hand chain is somewhat indirect, but the sightings were reportedly corroborated by multiple local witnesses.

**Sighting:** Witnesses described a silver-colored object, a flash of light/fire, and what looked like an airborne explosion followed by a falling object west of Ogden/Logan, near Taylor, Sardine Canyon, and west of Trenton. One report mentions two puffs of smoke high in the air; another says the object appeared to explode as it neared the mountain. The timing clustered around 9:00-9:20 AM on 5 Apr 1949.

**Investigation:** The report says the information was immediately furnished to OSI at Hill Field, Utah. Hill Field then advised that the phenomena were probably caused by two B-29s from Wendover Field practice-bombing in the desert west of Logan at extremely high altitude, producing vapor trails that could have been misread as aerial explosions or a falling disc. The document therefore records a UFO-style sighting but ends with a conventional military explanation rather than a confirmed unknown."

001_1949-04-16_Fort Smith, Arkansas (Nor.report_summary:
**Document:** FBI Office Memorandum (Standard Form No. 64) from the SAC, Little Rock, to the Director, FBI, dated 22 Apr 1949. The subject line reads “Unknown Subjects; Wade H. Harrison - Informant; Flying Discs; Fort Smith, Arkansas (4-16-49).” The page is marked with FBI exhibit/file notations including EX-118 and recorded/indexed stamps, indicating this is an internal investigative UFO report.

**Witness:** Wade H. Harrison of Fort Smith, Arkansas, whose residence is listed as Route 1, Box 293. He was employed as a Special Delivery messenger by the Fort Smith Post Office Department. The memo treats him as the principal civilian eyewitness, with no indication that he had prior involvement beyond providing the account.

**Sighting:** Harrison said that at about 5:25 p.m. on Saturday, 16 Apr 1949, while stopped at a traffic light at North Eleventh Street and Grand Avenue, he looked up and saw a “brilliant object” moving in a southeasterly direction. He estimated it was about 2 miles high and followed it for about 3 to 4 miles until trees blocked his view. He reported clear weather, good visibility, and no clouds near the object.

**Object:** The object made no audible noise. Harrison initially thought it might be a reflector on an airplane, but he could not locate or hear any aircraft. He also noted that other motorists nearby could have seen it when he pointed it out.

**Investigation:** After the sighting, Harrison later spoke with an Army officer wearing major or lieutenant colonel insignia at the 1400 block of North “C” Street. The officer said his wife had seen a similar flying object the day before while traveling from Oklahoma City toward Fort Smith, and that he had seen it too. The memo does not identify a final explanation, leaving the incident unresolved as a “flying discs” report rather than a confirmed aircraft or astronomical event.

The page also shows a May 3, 1949 communications-section stamp and routing/approval initials, indicating internal FBI handling rather than a field investigation.

Atkins in turn said that three employees of the Department of Recreation in Parks in the city of Los Angeles had seen objects in the sky that appeared to be flying discs. Because the observers are unnamed and the report is secondhand, witness credibility is limited to the confidential-source chain.

No precise time, direction, duration, altitude, number of objects, color, shape, speed, or maneuvering details are provided. The only description is that the objects in the sky “appeared to be flying discs.”

**Investigation:** The FBI explicitly states that the information is being furnished to the Air Force for any action desired and that “no investigation is being conducted” by the Bureau. Analytically, this is a brief referral, not a substantive case report: it preserves an early civilian UFO-style tip, but the page contains no corroboration, no technical description, and no follow-up findings.

001_1949-03-31_Killeen Base / Camp Hood.report_summary:
**Document:** FBI Office Memorandum (Standard Form No. 64), from the SAC, San Antonio, to the Director, FBI, dated April 4, 1949, marked "Air Mail / Special Delivery" and filed under Bureau file 65-48300 (with local notation 100-7545). The memo references an earlier San Antonio letter to the Bureau dated March 22, 1949 concerning "unconventional aircraft" and records a follow-up inquiry from G-2, 4th Army on April 4, 1949 asking whether the FBI had information to substantiate or discredit Walter Winchell’s remarks about "flying discs."

**Witness:** The principal observer was 1st Lt. Frederick W. Davis, who was in charge of a platoon in Company C, 12th Armored Infantry Battalion, part of the alert force ("Force Abel") assigned from Camp Hood to protect Killeen Base. The report presents him as a trained military officer on duty near the installation, which gives the account some operational credibility, though the narrative remains secondhand within the FBI memo.

**Sighting:** At about 11:50 P.M. on March 31, 1949, Lt. Davis reportedly saw a lighted object about the size of a basketball, reddish-white in color and trailing fire, southwest of Killeen Base adjacent to Camp Hood, Texas. He estimated it at about 6,000 feet altitude. The object traveled parallel to the ground, passed directly over him at rapid speed, remained visible for 10 to 15 seconds, and then suddenly disappeared high in the sky without descending. He reported no sound or odor, and the night was clear with good visibility. The object passed almost directly over the air strip at Killeen Base.

**Investigation:** Immediately after the sighting, Lt. Davis tried to telephone headquarters but heard static or electrical interference on the line, which he considered possibly radio interference. The memo further notes that G-2 reported other unidentified lights on March 6, 7, 8, and 17, 1949, seen by military personnel about 1,000 yards east of the fence surrounding Killeen Base, but states the March 31 object was different in nature from those earlier lights. No FBI analytic conclusion is recorded on this page; the document functions as a relay of military observations and a request for Bureau input amid public discussion of "flying discs."

001_1949-05-18_New Orleans, Louisiana_65.report_summary:
**Document:** One-page FBI Office Memorandum (Standard Form No. 64) from SAC, New Orleans to the Director, FBI, dated June 2, 1949, subject line “FLYING DISCS.” The memo references SAC Letter 38 of March 25, 1949 and carries Bureau routing/receipt stamps. It is an internal FBI intelligence note, not a field interview, and states that all three incidents had been investigated by Army Intelligence.

**Witness:** The underlying sightings were reported through the Office of Naval Intelligence, New Orleans, and involved two unnamed witnesses for at least one observation. The memo notes that the witnesses were outdoors and did not wear glasses. No personal names, occupations, or ranks are provided on this page.

**Sighting:** The Bureau was advised that three flying-disc sightings occurred in the City of New Orleans within the previous ten days, on May 18, 19, and 23, 1949. The objects were described as single discs in straight flight, generally northbound in the late afternoon, about the size of an observation plane but shaped like a saucer. The Navy further reported that two witnesses said the object appeared to be traveling end over end.

**Investigation:** Weather was reportedly good at the times of the sightings. Naval Intelligence considered the possibility that the objects were weather balloons, but noted that weather balloons were launched from only one airport, typically an hour before sighting times, and would usually be out of view within minutes. The memo does not reach a definitive conclusion, but it preserves the Navy’s tentative balloon explanation and the fact that Army Intelligence had already looked into the three cases. The event is therefore best catalogued as a New Orleans multi-sighting UFO/flying-disc report rather than a confirmed aircraft or astronomical identification.

A building manager said Marquardt had been employed by the Atomic Energy Commission. The FBI report does not reach a scientific conclusion; it simply records the Fire Marshal’s inquiry and the speculative UFO-related remark, leaving the incident unresolved on this page.

001_1947-07-01_Lake Ariel, Wayne County,.report_summary:

He said he was not present at the fire and had received the ash sample from a friend, **Woody Shaeffer** of Lake Ariel, Wayne County, by mail. His information is therefore secondhand, relaying Shaeffer's letter and sample rather than a direct observation.

**Sighting/incident:** Marquardt reported that Shaeffer's house, near **Lake Ariel** about one mile south of South Canaan, burned about six months earlier during a nighttime storm. According to Shaeffer's account, a **large object struck the roof** and ignited the house, which burned to the ground in less than an hour. Marquardt said the ash residue remained ignited for about twelve hours and that a quantity of ash was still on Shaeffer's premises.

**Object/analysis:** Kington furnished results of a city-laboratory analysis by Dr. Burke. The ash was said to contain **magnesium, aluminum, iron, calcium, silicates, sulphur, and carbonates**. **Investigation:** The report says the Marshal's Office withdrew on a question of jurisdiction and advised that any further action be referred to **State Police** authorities. 001_1954-09-05_Rockford, Illinois (moon.report_summary:
**Document:** This page is a mixed newsletter-style case-file page preserved in FBI file 62-HQ-83894, Section 8. It includes an unrelated write-up on the Cincinnati paint incident and, under **CASE FILE REVIEW**, a separate Rockford, Illinois observation coded “C-22, Rockford, Ill.. 9/5/54).” The page is numbered “-7-” and cites a prior article by Edward S. Schultz in B.S.R.A.’s *Round Robin*; the editorial note is signed by Meade Layne.

**Witness:** Amateur astronomers Peter Bartkus and Theodore McColm were watching the Moon through a telescope. Bartkus is the principal narrator in the quoted report.

**Sighting:** Between 10:35 and 11:15 P.M. on 5 September 1954, Bartkus reported observing “the most unusual phenomena” he had ever witnessed. The Moon was in first quarter, with an apparent diameter of 29 feet 30 inches. Using a 6-inch casigranian reflector telescope with secondary mirror, over 100 inches focal length, and 150x and 200x eyepieces, the pair saw a spherical object rising from the northern section of Mare Humboldtianum.

**Object:** The object was described as not glowing or brilliant, but more like a dull reflected light from a planet. Its estimated apparent size was about that of the craters Pitiscus or Vlaco. By the time it disappeared at 11:15 P.M. it had traversed more than the Moon’s apparent diameter in roughly 40 minutes.

**Investigation / conclusion:** The witnesses checked for atmospheric diffraction and optical artifacts by moving the telescope and changing eyepieces, but found no explanation. Bartkus concluded the object was a powered body because the Moon was descending at about 1,081 mph while the object appeared to rise and did not follow a true orbit. His final assessment was that it was “definitely in space” and in the same field as, or near, the Moon. The page records no formal FBI analysis beyond preserving the report in the case file.

Richards and are clearly part of the same incident/report, not separate events.

001_1944-01-01_Gut Alt Golssen (near Gol.report_summary:
**Document:** FBI Detroit 31, Michigan memorandum dated November 7, 1957, in file 62-83894-384, under the heading "UNIDENTIFIED FLYING OBJECTS." The page bears an unclassified stamp and red handwritten routing/approval notations. These two pages are a single continuous report; page 2 is explicitly marked "-2-" and continues the same interview narrative.

**Witness:** Wladyslav Krasuski, a Polish displaced person and former prisoner of war living in Detroit, was interviewed at the request of the federal government after writing to Robert Cutler, special assistant to President Dwight D. Eisenhower, saying he might know something about "the rocket in Texas." At the time of the interview he was employed at Gobel Brewery in Detroit.

**Sighting:** Krasuski said that in 1944, while walking to work near Gut Alt Golssen, about 30 miles east of Berlin, he experienced a tractor-engine stall in a swampy road area. He later observed an alleged circular vehicle in an otherwise deserted zone guarded by German SS personnel. He placed the vehicle at roughly 500 feet, describing it as circular, 75-100 yards across, about 14 feet high, with dark gray top and bottom sections and a three-foot middle section that appeared as a rapidly moving blurred band around the circumference. He also described a whine or generator-like noise.

**Investigation:** The account says an SS guard spoke with the tractor driver, waited several minutes, and the noise stopped, after which the tractor restarted normally. On a later visit, Krasuski said he saw a circular enclosure screened by a ~50-foot tarpaulin wall, a vertical rise of the object, and uninsulated metal cables running underground between the enclosure and a small concrete column-like structure. He reported that the cables were removed after the war and the area later flooded. The memo also notes he had not been in contact since 1945 with other POW laborers who had discussed the incident, except for remembering one man, Francizek Grabowski. The report is a retrospective wartime recollection, not a contemporaneous airborne sighting, and the source is a single civilian witness with no corroboration in the file excerpt.

001_1960-02-21_Grand Blanc, Michigan (Ed.report_summary:
**Document:** FBI Detroit memorandum dated March 9, 1960, headed "Re: Unidentified Flying Object; Joseph Perry, Grand Blanc, Michigan – Complaint." It is a narrative report in Bureau correspondence style, produced in response to Perry’s request. The page is part of FBI case file 62-HQ-83894, Section 9.

**Witness:** Joseph Perry of 3079 Edwards Street, Grand Blanc, Michigan, said he operated a pizza house at 3075 Edwards Street and had been a professional photographer for about thirty years. Agents contacted him at his request on March 5, 1960.

**Sighting:** Perry reported that at about 1:00 a.m. on February 21, 1960, while photographing the moon through a home-made telescope, he took a set of moon photographs. After developing them and viewing the images, he said that one photograph showed what appeared to be a flying object somewhere between the end of the telescope and the surface of the moon.

**Object:** Perry described the object as flat on the bottom when enlarged, oval-shaped, with a fluorescent glow around the entire object and a vapor trail behind it. He believed it was actually moving. He said he had taken over 1,000 moon pictures and had never seen anything resembling it. Based on his photographic experience, he stated he was sure the image was not a camera malfunction, not a blur from the telescope, and not an artifact of film development.

**Investigation:** Perry said he took about twenty moon pictures that night, found most underexposed, cut out the two that appeared properly exposed, destroyed the rest, and furnished both selected pictures to the FBI. The page contains Perry’s statement only and does not record any final Bureau conclusion about the image.

**Document:** FBI Cincinnati memorandum/letter dated October 17, 1961, file no. 100-11671, with the subject line "Civilian Research, Interplanetary Flying Objects, Leonard H. Stringfield, Director, Cincinnati, Ohio." The page bears a loan stamp indicating it was circulated by the FBI.

**Witness:** Leonard H. Stringfield was identified as an advertising manager for DuBois Chemical Company, Inc., and as a well-known civilian UFO researcher. The letter notes that he lived at 4412 Grove Avenue, Mariemont, Cincinnati, Ohio, had published a UFO bulletin, and had worked with the Air Defense Command on matters involving unidentified flying objects.

**Event:** Stringfield said he appeared on the television program *Impact News* on WCPO-TV, Cincinnati, on Sunday, September 10, 1961. He reported that at approximately 9:00 A.M. on September 25, 1961, he received an anonymous telephone call from a male caller whose voice he described as firm, clear, and speaking good English. The caller said he had very important information to relate to Stringfield about unidentified flying objects and asked for Stringfield by name.

**Investigation:** This page is an FBI record of Stringfield’s account, not a UFO observation report with object characteristics. The extant text ends mid-narrative, and no corroboration, analysis, or conclusion appears on this page. The report mainly documents Stringfield’s background, his media appearance, and the anonymous UFO-related contact he received.

001_1961-10-15_Cincinnati, Ohio (Mr. Str.report_summary:
**Document:** Declassified FBI case file 62-HQ-83894, Section 9, typed continuation page marked “-2-” (page 0189). This page contains the second half of an FBI memorandum/report; no signature or report date is visible on the page shown, but it is clearly part of an FBI file concerning UFO-related correspondence and calls.

**Witness:** Leonard H. Stringfield, identified here as a public UFO researcher and adviser to the National Investigations Committee on Aerial Phenomena (NICAP). He also stated that he was authorized to report unidentified-object sightings to Air Defense Command headquarters in Columbus, Ohio, which the report uses to explain why he may receive such calls.

**Sighting/Claim:** Stringfield described a telephone call from an unidentified male who refused to identify himself but, according to Stringfield, spoke intelligently and did not sound like a prankster. The caller told him to expect “the biggest flurry of unidentified flying objects sightings” as a result of Russian nuclear explosions “in the one hundred megaton range.” He advised that confusion would begin with these sightings and said, “Mark these dates, October 15 to October 19,” adding that this would be the greatest UFO incident “over the years.” The caller reportedly said he would remain in touch and call back after the nineteenth.

**Assessment:** Stringfield told the FBI he was concerned because the caller seemed serious and because, if true, such a claim could cause public panic. He emphasized that anonymous UFO-related calls were not unusual for him due to his public role. The page records no confirmed visual observation, only an anonymous prediction/warning; the available text does not support any verified UFO event and reads more like an unverified tip or hoax warning than a substantiated sighting.

001_1947-04-26_Unspecified rural New Mex.report_summary:
**Document:** FBI UFO case-file page 2 from 62-HQ-83894, Section 9. The page is a typed continuation marked “PAGE TWO / END PAGE TWO” and ends with a referral to the proper military authorities at Kirtland AFB, Albuquerque.

**Witness:** The initial observer is identified only as Orlando, a civilian local resident. On this page he appears to have been dismissed by his father when he first reported the event. A New Mexico State Police officer, Captain Vigil, later inspected the site and provided physical observations.

**Sighting:** Orlando reportedly saw a blue-white flame that appeared to come from “port holes” on a stationary, silent object. He watched for about one minute until the flame went out. He then went into the house, told his father, and returned the next morning to find a smoldering area at the site.

**Object / Ground Effects:** Captain Vigil said he checked the site at about 7:30 PM on April 26. He noted a scorched circular area roughly 30–40 feet in diameter, one rectangular/V-shaped indentation in the ground about 8 by 12 inches and 3–4 inches deep, and three more similar indentations reported by another officer. He also saw several smooth circular prints on the ground about 3.5 inches across.

**Investigation:** The excerpt names no other witnesses and provides no identification of the object. The physical traces make the report more substantial than a simple visual sighting, but the file fragment does not establish a cause. The event remains unresolved in this excerpt; possibilities could include a landing or burn event, but no firm conclusion is documented here.
